rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya places the verse in the staged prohibition of wine, citing the later commands to avoid it and the Prophet’s declaration that it was forbidden.
rows.anchor: إنما الخمر والميسر والأنصاب والأزلام رجس من عمل الشيطان فاجتنبوه

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet declared wine forbidden; Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives no grading for this report.
rows.anchor: فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «حرمت الخمر»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The only preserved Prophetic practice on the wine penalty is forty lashes, reported by Muslim and Abū Dāwūd.
rows.anchor: ولم يحفظ عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في حد الخمر إلا أنه جلد أربعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says the Prophet administered an unspecified general beating; Abū Bakr estimated it at forty, followed by Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: وروي عنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه ضرب فيها ضربا مشاعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As drinking spread, ʿUmar raised the penalty to eighty as the lightest fixed penalty; Mālik agreed, while al-Shāfiʿī held to forty.
rows.anchor: ثم تهافت الناس فيها فشدد عليهم الحد وجعله كأخف الحدود ثمانين

rows.speaker: جماعة من العلماء
rows.claim: A group of scholars required a non-severe beating, such that the striker’s armpit would not show.
rows.anchor: وضرب الخمر غير شديد عند جماعة من العلماء لا يبدو إبط الضارب

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik says every flogging should use the same force, without easing it or striking excessively.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك: «الضرب كله سواء لا يخفف ولا يبرح»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is consensus to avoid striking the face, genitals, heart, brain, and flanks of the person flogged.
rows.anchor: ويجتنب من المضروب الوجه والفرج والقلب والدماغ والخواصر بإجماع

rows.speaker: طائفة
rows.claim: Some say the verse’s apparent allowance in mentioning benefits was abrogated by the command to avoid wine and gambling.
rows.anchor: وقالت طائفة: هذه الآية منسوخة بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maysir derives from y-s-r in the sense of slaughtering; yāsir means the slaughterer, and the camel subject to the draw was called maysir, then the arrows by association.
rows.anchor: والميسر مأخوذ من يسر إذا جزر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two cited poetic lines use y-s-r language for the slaughter-and-lottery practice, supporting the derivation from slaughter.
rows.anchor: فلم يزل بك واشيهم ومكرهم ... حتى أشاطوا بغيب لحم من يسروا

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī derives maysir from “this became due or available to me” and attributes that etymology to Mujāhid; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says Mujāhid’s quoted words instead mean slaughter.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري: «الميسر مأخوذ من يسر لي هذا إذا وجب وتسنى»

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid’s intended sense was slaughter; a yāsir is someone who participates in drawing lots, plural aysār (also described as yusr).
rows.anchor: بل أراد مجاهد الجزر، واليسر: الذي يدخل في الضرب بالقداح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lottery used seven arrows with assigned shares and three blanks without shares: al-fadhdh, al-tawʾam, al-raqīb, al-ḥils, al-nāfis, al-musbil, al-muʿallā; al-manīḥ, al-safīḥ, and al-waghd were blanks.
rows.anchor: وسهام الميسر سبعة لها حظوظ وفيها فروض على عدة الحظوظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three blank arrows were added to multiply and mix the lots so the person drawing them could not favor anyone.
rows.anchor: والثلاثة التي لا حظوظ لها المنيح والسفيح والوغد، تزاد هذه الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabs used this practice in winter scarcity and severe cold: participants guaranteed the camel’s price, slaughtered it, and divided it into ten portions; al-Aṣmaʿī’s claim of twenty-eight portions is mistaken.
rows.anchor: وكانت عادة العرب أن تضرب بهذه القداح في الشتوة وضيق الوقت وكلب البرد على الفقراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A winning arrow took its allotted shares for the poor; sometimes participants gambled for themselves, and those who lost paid the price. The practice sustained the neighborhood’s poor.
rows.anchor: فمن فاز سهمه بأن يخرج من الربابة متقدما أخذ أنصباءه وأعطاها الفقراء

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿshā’s verse praises the lottery’s provision of food to guests and the poor in winter, illustrating its social benefit.
rows.anchor: المطعمو الضيف إذا ما شتا ... والجاعلو القوت على الياسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These customs were benefits of maysir, but the practice still consumed wealth unlawfully.
rows.anchor: فهذا كله هو نفع الميسر، إلا أنه أكل المال بالباطل،

rows.speaker: محمد بن سيرين والحسن وابن عباس وابن المسيب وغيرهم
rows.claim: They classify every form of gambling as maysir, including dice, chess, and even children’s nut games.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن سيرين والحسن وابن عباس وابن المسيب وغيرهم: كل قمار ميسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a cited poem, al-manīḥ is a borrowed, smooth arrow that had won often; this favorable loan-arrow differs from the blank manīḥ, which is praised for its turning back.
rows.anchor: والمنيح في هذا البيت المستمنح، لأنهم كانوا يستعيرون السهم

rows.speaker: جرير
rows.claim: Jarīr’s line uses al-manīḥ for the blank arrow, described as one that turns back, rather than the lucky borrowed arrow.
rows.anchor: وإياه أراد جرير بقوله: [الكامل] ولقد عطفن على فزارة

rows.speaker: لبيد
rows.claim: Labīd’s line says the lottery need not produce shameful acts, another poetic illustration of the practice’s benefits before the Qurʾānic judgment of its sin.
rows.anchor: ومن الميسر قول لبيد: [الطويل] إذا يسروا لم يورث اليسر بينهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والربيع
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Rabīʿ say the sin concerns wine and gambling after prohibition, while their benefits belonged to the earlier period.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس والربيع: الإثم فيهما بعد التحريم

rows.speaker: طائفة
rows.claim: One group locates wine’s sin in loss of reason, abuse, slander, harm, and transgression by drinkers, and its benefit in pleasure.
rows.anchor: وقالت طائفة: الإثم في الخمر ذهاب العقل والسباب والافتراء

rows.speaker: حسان بن ثابت
rows.claim: Ḥassān b. Thābit’s poem depicts wine as making drinkers feel like kings and fearless lions, illustrating the pleasure claimed as its benefit.
rows.anchor: كما قال حسان بن ثابت: ونشربها فتتركنا ملوكا ... وأسدا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the benefit of wine as the money earned from its sale.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: «المنفعة بها كسب أثمانها»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God says the sin outweighs the benefit and brings greater harm in the afterlife; Ibn ʿAṭiyya reads this comparison as a prelude to prohibition.
rows.anchor: ثم أعلم الله عز وجل أن الإثم أكبر من النفع وأعود بالضرر في الآخرة

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read kathīr (“many”); the Prophet’s curse on wine and ten connected roles supports many sins, as does pairing plural benefits with plural sins.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي «كثير» بالثاء المثلثة

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet cursed wine and ten associated people: its seller, buyer, purchaser for another, pressers, those for whom it is pressed, server, drinker, carrier, recipient, and one who consumes its price; Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives no grading.
rows.anchor: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لعن الخمر ولعن معها عشرة

rows.speaker: جمهور الناس
rows.claim: Most readers use kabīr (“great”), fitting wine and gambling as major sins and the following akbar (“greater”); they reject akthar except in Ibn Masʿūd’s codex, which has kathīr in both places.
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي القراء وجمهور الناس «كبير» بالباء بواحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The codex attributed to Ibn Masʿūd reads kathīr (“many”) at both occurrences, unlike the mainstream agreement on akbar and rejection of akthar.
rows.anchor: إلا ما في مصحف ابن مسعود فإن فيه «قل فيهما إثم كثير وإثمهما أكثر»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In them is sin” may mean sin in using wine and gambling after the prohibition, or the evil qualities inherent in them.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: فيهما إثم يحتمل مقصدين، أحدهما أن يراد في استعمالهما

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd b. Jubayr recounts a staged response: after this verse some abstained for sin while others drank for benefit; 4:43 restricted drinking around prayers, then 5:90 commanded avoidance and the Prophet declared wine forbidden.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير: لما نزلت قل فيهما إثم كبير ومنافع للناس

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: When 5:91 asked whether they would desist, ʿUmar answered that they had desisted; Ibn ʿAṭiyya uses this as the final step in the prohibition sequence.
rows.anchor: ولما سمع عمر بن الخطاب قوله تعالى: فهل أنتم منتهون

rows.speaker: بعض أهل النظر
rows.claim: Some speculative scholars infer that this verse itself prohibited wine: 7:33 forbids sin, and this verse says wine contains sin.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض أهل النظر: حرمت الخمر بهذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects that inference: the sin found in wine is what is forbidden, not wine itself as that argument requires.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد عبد الحق رضي الله عنه: ليس هذا النظر بجيد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the verse censured wine but did not prohibit it.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: ذم الله الخمر بهذه الآية ولم يحرمها

rows.speaker: قيس بن سعد
rows.claim: Qays b. Saʿd interprets “the surplus” to be the obligatory alms tax.
rows.anchor: قال قيس بن سعد: «هذه الزكاة المفروضة»

rows.speaker: جمهور العلماء
rows.claim: Most scholars interpret the spending requested here as voluntary expenditure.
rows.anchor: وقال جمهور العلماء: بل هي نفقات التطوع

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say the command to spend the surplus was abrogated by the later zakat obligation.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: نسخت بالزكاة

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others hold the verse remains in force and establishes a claim on wealth beyond zakat.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون: هي محكمة وفي المال حق سوى الزكاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿafw is what one can give without exhausting oneself or one’s assets: spend what remains after needs, without making oneself dependent; the term derives from abundance.
rows.anchor: والعفو: هو ما ينفقه المرء دون أن يجهد نفسه وماله

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic report directs a person with surplus to spend first on self, then dependents, then charity if anything remains; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: روي أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: قال: «من كان له فضل فلينفقه على نفسه، ثم على من يعول

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Two Prophetic reports commend charity that leaves the giver financially secure, described as giving from sufficiency; Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives no grading.
rows.anchor: وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم: «خير الصدقة ما أبقت غنى» ، وفي حديث آخر

rows.speaker: جمهور الناس وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: Most readers put al-ʿafw in the accusative; Abū ʿAmr alone raises it, and Ibn Kathīr’s reading is reported as differing.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور الناس «العفو» بالنصب، وقرأ أبو عمرو وحده «العفو» بالرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If mā is a subject and dhā its relative predicate, al-ʿafw is nominative; if mādhā is one object of “spend,” al-ʿafw is accusative after an implied verb. The mixed case pairings are possible but weak.
rows.anchor: فمن جعل «ما» ابتداء و «ذا» خبره بمعنى الذي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Thus God makes the signs clear” refers to the preceding discussions of wine, gambling, and spending; the signs guide believers to reflect on worldly and afterlife matters as a path to salvation.
rows.anchor: الإشارة إلى ما تقدم تبيينه من أمر الخمر والميسر والإنفاق

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makkī reads “in this world and the next” as modifying “the signs,” while the familiar interpretation associated with Ibn ʿAbbās attaches it to “reflect.”
rows.anchor: وقال مكي: «معنى الآية أنه يبين للمؤمنين آيات في الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Have you not seen?” is an admonition using the vision of the heart, not physical sight.
rows.anchor: ألم تر تنبيه، وهي رؤية القلب

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib read the final rāʾ of “alam tara” with sukūn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علي بن أبي طالب «ألم تر» بجزم الراء

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة والربيع والسدي وابن إسحاق وزيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: The disputant was Nimrod son of Canaan, son of Cush, son of Shem, son of Noah, the contemporary king associated with the fire and the mosquito.
rows.anchor: هذا قول مجاهد وقتادة والربيع والسدي وابن إسحاق وزيد بن أسلم وغيرهم

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj identifies Nimrod as the first king on earth; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this is rejected.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج: هو أول ملك في الأرض وهذا مردود

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda calls Nimrod the first tyrant and the builder or owner of the tower at Babylon.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: هو أول من تجبر وهو صاحب الصرح ببابل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other accounts give Nimrod a different lineage, as son of Falikh, son of ʿĀmir, son of Shalikh, son of Arfakhshadh, son of Shem, son of Noah.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن الذي حاج إبراهيم نمرود بن فالخ بن عامر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say Nimrod ruled the whole world; he was one of two great disbelievers, the other being Nebuchadnezzar.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه ملك الدنيا بأجمعها ونفذت فيها طينته وهو أحد الكافرين

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: In Zayd b. Aslam’s account, Nimrod controlled food distributions and demanded that visitors name their lord; when Abraham answered, Nimrod claimed to give life and death, then denied him provisions after the sun challenge.
rows.anchor: ذكر زيد بن أسلم أن النمرود هذا قعد يأمر للناس بالميرة

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: After leaving without provisions, Abraham wished to bring home sand so his children could play; his wife found fine flour in one sack, and Abraham recognized this as God’s provision.
rows.anchor: فعلم إبراهيم أن الله تعالى يسر لهم ذلك،

rows.speaker: الربيع وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Rabīʿ and others say Nimrod summoned two men, killed one and released the other, claiming he had caused one death and one life; Abraham answered with the sunrise challenge, leaving him stunned.
rows.anchor: وقال الربيع وغيره في هذه القصص:

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says that after Abraham emerged from the fire, Nimrod asked his lord; Nimrod claimed life and death by starving four men, feeding two and leaving two to die, before Abraham challenged him about the sun.
rows.anchor: ذكر السدي: أنه لما خرج إبراهيم من النار أدخلوه على الملك

rows.speaker: الأصوليون
rows.claim: The legal theorists say Abraham meant life and death literally as divine attributes, while Nimrod exploited a figurative sense to mislead his people; Abraham yielded for argument’s sake, then used a sun example admitting no figurative evasion.
rows.anchor: وذكر الأصوليون في هذه الآية: أن إبراهيم عليه السلام وصف ربه تعالى بما هو صفة له

words: فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَأْتِى بِٱلشَّمْسِ مِنَ ٱلْمَشْرِقِ
rows.speaker: الأصوليون
rows.claim: The theorists add that Nimrod could not claim to bring the sun from the east because the people would call him a liar.
rows.anchor: ولم يمكنه أن يقول: أنا الآتي بها من المشرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb ḥājja is on the fāʿala pattern from ḥujja, meaning that the disputant contended with Abraham over the proof.
rows.anchor: وقوله حاج وزنه «فاعل» من الحجة أي جاذبه إياها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “his Lord” may refer either to Abraham or to the disputant.
rows.anchor: والضمير في ربه يحتمل أن يعود على إبراهيم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An ā-tāhu is causal (“because He gave him”); most commentators take the pronoun in ā-tāhu to mean Nimrod.
rows.anchor: وأن مفعول من أجله والضمير في آتاه للنمرود

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī suggests the pronoun refers to Abraham, who was given the kingship of prophethood; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this an overstrained interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقال المهدوي: يحتمل أن يعود الضمير على إبراهيم أن آتاه ملك النبوءة

rows.speaker: جمهور القراء ونافع
rows.claim: Most readers drop the alif of anā in connected recitation; Nāfiʿ’s transmitters Warsh, Ibn Abī Uways, and Qālūn retain it before a following hamza, except in 7:188 and 26:115.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور القراء أن أحيي بطرح الألف التي بعد النون من أنا

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī explains that anā consists of hamza and nūn with an alif added in pause; in liaison the following word takes the alif’s place, as with the pause hāʾ and the form ḥayyahlā.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: ضمير المتكلم الاسم فيه الهمزة والنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the alif resembles one added in poetic rhyme; Abū ʿAlī says it drops when the word is joined, though the following word fills its role.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد: وهذا مثال الألف التي تلحق في القوافي، فتأمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic line preserves the alif in connected anā, illustrating the exceptional retention discussed by the grammarians.
rows.anchor: أنا شيخ العشيرة فاعرفوني ... حميدا قد تذريت السناما

rows.speaker: جمهور القراء
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce buhita with ḍamma on bāʾ and kasra on hāʾ, meaning the opponent was silenced and overcome by proof.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: «فبهت» الذي بضم الباء وكسر الهاء

rows.speaker: ابن سيده
rows.claim: Ibn Sīda reports two other forms for being stunned: bahti with both opening and kasra on hāʾ, and buhita with opened bāʾ and ḍamma on hāʾ.
rows.anchor: قال ابن سيده: ويقال في هذا المعنى: «بهت» بفتح الباء وكسر الهاء

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī reports that some Arabs used bahta with both bāʾ and hāʾ opened for this meaning.
rows.anchor: قال الطبري: وحكي عن بعض العرب في هذا المعنى، «بهت» بفتح الباء والهاء

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥaywa reads with opened bāʾ and ḍamma on hāʾ, a dialectal form of the reading with kasra on hāʾ.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو حيوة: «فبهت» بفتح الباء وضم الهاء

rows.speaker: ابن السميفع
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sumayfiʿ reads both consonants opened, construing the phrase as Abraham stunning the disbeliever, with “the one who disbelieved” as the object; it may also be a dialect variant.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن السميفع: «فبهت» بفتح الباء والهاء

rows.speaker: الأخفش وابن جني
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash reports a kasra-on-hāʾ reading like khariqa and dahisha; Ibn Jinnī says the more common ḍamma intensifies the meaning.
rows.anchor: وحكى أبو الحسن الأخفش قراءة «فبهت» بكسر الهاء كخرق ودهش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpreted the both-open reading as Nimrod abusing or cursing Abraham after being silenced and left without an answer.
rows.anchor: وقد تأول قوم في قراءة من قرأ فبهت بفتحهما أنه بمعنى سب وقذف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing statement addresses Muḥammad and his community: God does not guide people in arguments while they persist in wrongdoing, since wrongdoing has no guidance.
rows.anchor: إخبار لمحمد عليه السلام وأمته. والمعنى: لا يرشدهم في حججهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although phrased generally, the warning is particular: God may guide wrongdoers who repent and return to faith; alternatively, it concerns those who meet God still unjust.
rows.anchor: فظاهره العموم، ومعناه الخصوص، كما ذكرنا، لأن الله قد يهدي الظالمين بالتوبة

rows.speaker: نافع وعاصم
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ and ʿĀṣim read yuʿallimuhu with yāʾ; Abū ʿAlī connects it to “he gives you glad tidings” at 3:45, or allows it as a circumstantial clause after “he speaks” at 3:46.
rows.anchor: قرأ نافع وعاصم «ويعلمه» بالياء، وذلك عطف على يبشرك بكلمة

rows.speaker: باقي القراء
rows.claim: The other readers use nuʿallimuhu with the majestic first-person plural; the meaning matches the yāʾ reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الباقون، و «نعلمه» بالنون، وهي مثل قراءة الياء في المعنى

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī attaches the yāʾ reading to 3:47 and the nūn reading to 3:44; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects both analyses as grammatically and semantically wrong.
rows.anchor: قال الطبري: قراءة الياء عطف على قوله: يخلق ما يشاء

rows.speaker: ابن جريج وجماعة المفسرين
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj and a group of commentators take “the Book” to mean writing by hand, the verbal noun of kataba.
rows.anchor: والكتاب هو الخط باليد فهو مصدر كتب يكتب، هذا قول ابن جريج

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say “the Book” points to an unspecified revealed book; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects this as a claim without evidence.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: هي إشارة إلى كتاب منزل لم يعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wisdom is prophetic Sunna in law, exhortation, and similar matters not revealed through a book or angel, but inspired and supported by sound dispositions; other scholars define it as rightness in speech and action.
rows.anchor: وأما الحكمة، فهي السنة التي يتكلم بها الأنبياء، في الشرعيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus can be taught wisdom received by revelation or inherited from earlier prophets and scholars; his distinctive wisdom is prepared through aptitude, practice, and capacity to derive it.
rows.anchor: والتعليم متمكن فيما كان من الحكمة بوحي أو مأثورا عمن تقدم عيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah is the revelation given to Moses; reports say Jesus mastered it and acted on it more fully than others.
rows.anchor: والتوراة هي المنزلة على موسى عليه السلام، ويروى أن عيسى كان يستظهر التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says only Moses, Joshua b. Nun, ʿUzayr, and Jesus memorized the Torah by heart; Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives no grading.
rows.anchor: ويروى أنه لم يحفظها عن ظهر قلب إلا أربعة، موسى ويوشع بن نون وعزيز وعيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Gospel was mentioned to Mary before it descended because it was already known among prophets and scholars as a book that would be sent down.
rows.anchor: وذكر الإنجيل لمريم وهو ينزل- بعد- لأنه كان كتابا مذكورا عند الأنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “As a messenger” may be a circumstantial clause coordinated with “he teaches him,” or imply “He makes him a messenger”; semantically the whole description connects to “held in honor” at 3:45.
rows.anchor: وقوله: ورسولا حال معطوفة على ويعلمه إذ التقدير، ومعلما الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus was sent to the Israelites to explain Torah law, call them to follow it, and make lawful some things it had forbidden, including certain foods, camel meat, and some fish and birds.
rows.anchor: وكانت رسالة عيسى عليه السلام إلى بني إسرائيل، مبينا حكم التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The speech to Mary runs through “Israel”; the words “I have come to you” through “straight path” are most naturally what Jesus will say to Israel, with an understood “then Jesus came and said” afterward. An alternative places that omitted transition before the speech.
rows.anchor: والأول أظهر، وقرأ جمهور الناس «أني قد جئتكم» بفتح الألف

rows.speaker: جمهور الناس
rows.claim: Most readers open the hamza of annī, understood as bi-annī (“that I have come”); an irregular reading uses innī with kasra.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور الناس «أني قد جئتكم» بفتح الألف

rows.speaker: جمهور الناس
rows.claim: Most readers have the singular “a sign”; Ibn Masʿūd’s codex has the plural “signs,” also in the later phrase “I have come to you with signs from your Lord.”
rows.anchor: وجمهور الناس قرؤوا بآية على الإفراد وفي مصحف ابن مسعود «بآيات»

rows.speaker: نافع وجماعة من العلماء
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ and a group read innī with kasra, either as a new independent statement or as an explanation of the sign, like the Adam example.
rows.anchor: فقرأ نافع وجماعة من العلماء، «إني» بكسر الألف

rows.speaker: باقي السبعة وجماعة من العلماء
rows.claim: The remaining canonical readers and other scholars open the hamza: “that I shape,” as an apposition to “a sign” or to the first annī; these parses are close in meaning.
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة وجماعة من العلماء، «أني» بفتح الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here akhluqu means to shape, measure, or prepare by hand, as in Zuhayr’s line contrasting shaping something with successfully completing it.
rows.anchor: وأخلق معناه، أقدر وأهيئ بيدي، ومن ذلك قول الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “For you” qualifies the shaping and shows that Jesus does not claim creation from nothing; the clause “by God’s permission” makes this explicit.
rows.anchor: وقوله لكم تقييد لقوله، أخلق لأنه يدل دلالة ما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation properly concerns physical bodies but is also used figuratively, as at 29:17 for inventing falsehood and in a cited poem for making up speech.
rows.anchor: وحقيقة الخلق في الأجرام، ويستعمل في المعاني، ومنه قوله تعالى: وتخلقون إفكا

words: فَأَنفُخُ فِيهِ فَيَكُونُ طَيْرًۢا بِإِذْنِ ٱللَّهِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus shapes the clay and breathes to show his involvement in the sign; God alone brings the form into existence from nothing and creates life in it.
rows.anchor: وأما الإيجاد من العدم وخلق الحياة في ذلك الطين فمن الله تعالى وحده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use hayʾa, on the faʿla pattern, from a verb meaning to settle or take an ordered state, and it is made transitive as hayyaʾa.
rows.anchor: وجمهور الناس قرأ «كهيئة» على وزن فعلة بفتح الفاء

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrī reads hayʾati with kasra on hāʾ and a geminated, opened yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الزهري «كهيئة الطير» ، بكسر الهاء وياء مفتوحة مشددة

words: كَهَيْـَٔةِ ٱلطَّيْرِ فَأَنفُخُ فِيهِ فَيَكُونُ طَيْرًۢا
rows.speaker: أبو جعفر بن القعقاع
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar b. al-Qaʿqāʿ reads “bird” as singular in both places: the first is a collective genus and the second means one bird among birds.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر بن القعقاع، «كهيئة الطائر فأنفخ فيه فيكون طائرا»

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ alone uses singular ṭāʾiran in the final position; the other readers use plural ṭayran in both places, likewise in Sūrat al-Māʾida.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وحده، «كهيئة الطير فأنفخ فيه فيكون طائرا» بالإفراد في الأخير

rows.speaker: أبو علي عن أبي الحسن
rows.claim: Ṭayr is a collective noun, not a standard plural form; the regular plural of ṭāʾir is aṭyār, and the plural of that is ṭuyūr.
rows.anchor: والطير اسم جمع وليس من أبنية الجموع، وإنما البناء في جمع طائر أطيار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine pronoun in “I breathe into it” can refer to the prepared clay or to the previously mentioned object.
rows.anchor: وقوله فأنفخ فيه ذكر الضمير هنا لأنه يحتمل أن يعود على الطين المهيأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 5:110 the pronoun is feminine, referring either to the form (hayʾa) or to the feminine collective wording for birds.
rows.anchor: وأنث الضمير في سورة المائدة في قوله، فتنفخ فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Permission means God’s knowledge that the act will occur and His enabling it; accompanying speech makes the permission more explicit and can approach a command, though it remains within permission.
rows.anchor: وقوله بإذن الله، معناه بعلم منه تعالى أني أفعل ذلك وتمكين منه لي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya links the phrase to “they defeated them by God’s permission” at 2:251 and cites the Prophetic dictum that a woman’s silence is her permission.
rows.anchor: وتأمل قوله تعالى: فهزموهم بإذن الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraʾu means to remove illness: a patient may be described as healed, and one person may heal another.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: أبرئ، معناه أزيل المرض يقال برأ المريض وأبرأه غيره

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid defines an akmah as someone who sees in daylight but not at night.
rows.anchor: فقال مجاهد: الأكمه هو الذي يبصر بالنهار ولا يبصر بالليل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن والسدي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and al-Suddī define akmah as absolutely blind.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس والحسن والسدي: الأكمه الأعمى على الإطلاق

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says an akmah is someone with weak or dim eyesight.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: الأكمه الأعمش

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqāsh reports a view that akmah means mute and unable to understand, “dead of heart.”
rows.anchor: وحكى النقاش قولا: أن الأكمه هو الأبكم الذي لا يفهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda also define akmah as someone born blind, with closed eyes.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا وقتادة: الأكمه الذي يولد أعمى مضموم العين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus healed every illness by prayer and touch, but a prophetic proof must concern ailments beyond physicians; the born-blind definition best fits, since akmah linguistically means blind. Without that linguistic constraint, al-Naqqāsh’s sense would make a good proof.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي: وقد كان عيسى عليه السلام يبرىء بدعائه ومسح يده كل علة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Leprosy is a familiar disease and, once established, does not heal.
rows.anchor: والأبرص معروف، وهو داء لا يبرأ منه إذا تمكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports say Jesus struck a dead person, grave, or skull with his staff, reviving a person who then spoke; no specific authority is given.
rows.anchor: وروي في إحيائه الموتى، أنه كان يضرب بعصاه الميت أو القبر أو الجمجمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says Jesus raised Sam, son of Noah; other accounts disagree over whether the revived person remained alive or soon died again.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه أحيى سام بن نوح عليه السلام، وروي أن الذي كان يحييه كانت تدوم حياته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says there are many resurrection stories, but their reports cannot be established as authentic.
rows.anchor: وفي قصص الإحياء أحاديث كثيرة لا يوقف على صحتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raising the dead is Jesus’s miraculous sign exposed to challenge in substance, even though the verse does not explicitly state the challenge.
rows.anchor: وإحياء الموتى هي آيته المعجزة المعرضة للتحدي، وهي بالمعنى متحدى بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus’s signs addressed the age’s preoccupation with medicine: healing and raising the dead exceeded humoral theory and medical practice, revealing divine power, just as Moses challenged magicians and Muḥammad challenged masters of eloquence.
rows.anchor: وآيات عيسى عليه السلام إنما تجري فيما يعارض الطب لأن علم الطب كان شرف الناس

words: أَخْلُقُ لَكُم مِّنَ ٱلطِّينِ كَهَيْـَٔةِ ٱلطَّيْرِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A story says Jesus asked which bird was hardest to form; the Israelites chose the featherless bat, so he shaped clay bats and breathed life into them before witnesses, who called him a magician. No authority or grading is given.
rows.anchor: فيقولون: الخفاش، لأنه طائر لا ريش له
